Subject: First-token targets & streaming cadence — post-demo next steps

Hi Emma and Ryan,

Thanks again for the demo earlier — really helpful to see the FastPay use-cases. Per our conversation, I wanted to capture the key performance goals you called out and propose concrete next steps so we can size a PoC. High-level asks from the call:

- TTFT (Time-to-first-token): strict interactive target, p95 <= 70 ms (ideally p50 ~ 35–45 ms) for single-turn chat.
- Streaming: server->client streaming over SSE or WebSocket with first chunk within the TTFT window and subsequent chunk cadence smooth enough to replicate a typing UX (rough target: chunks every 80–120 ms).
- Concurrency/throughput: support ~200 concurrent interactive sessions at peak, sustained throughput target ~120 requests/sec, with spikes to 250 rps for short bursts.
- Degradation: graceful fallback to a lower-cost variant (same model family/quant) when capacity constrained; no hard failures to the user.

Next steps I propose:
1) Dylan to propose runtime/config recommendations and pre-warm sizing for a 2-week PoC (action: Dylan)
2) We’ll share an SLO matrix and network requirements (attached draft) and a short PoC success criteria doc.
3) Schedule a 30-minute follow-up with your infra owners to confirm network egress and websocket/SSE paths — propose Wed May 20, 9am PT.

Attachments: SLO_matrix_v1.xlsx, redwood-network-topology.png

If any of the goals above don’t reflect your requirements, call them out and I’ll update.

Cheers,

Thanks Neha — this matches what we discussed. A few clarifications from our infra/product side:

- TTFT: our product PM wants p95 <= 60–70ms for the first token for the core payment auth flow (this is non-negotiable for the user experience on slow networks).
- Streaming cadence: our UX lead cares more about perceived responsiveness than exact ms — they asked if we can guarantee first chunk within TTFT and then steady updates around every 100ms for the first 1–2s, then back off to 200–300ms for longer outputs.
- Chunk sizing: low overhead per chunk preferred. We’re targeting ~8–20 tokens per chunk.
- Concurrency: 180–220 simultaneous end-users during peak hours (US east), plus background batch scoring jobs off-peak.

Question: do you recommend SSE or WebSocket for our web clients? We use a mix — some mobile/embedded webviews prefer WebSocket.

Also looping in Ryan (infra) — he’ll confirm network egress and TLS termination details.

—Emma

From: Dylan Brooks <dylan.brooks@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: First-token targets & streaming cadence — post-demo next steps

Hi Emma/Ryan — quick technical response with recommended config and trade-offs. TL;DR: we can meet the TTFT/streaming goals with a mix of pre-warmed workers, small-batch serving, and a streaming-optimized kernel profile.

Key recommendations:
- Serving mode: Dedicated pre-warm pool (Redwood Dedicated) sized for interactive SLOs. Cold starts are the biggest TTFT hit — pre-warmed workers eliminate that.
- Model variant + quant: use a 4-bit or 8-bit quantized variant we’ve validated for streaming; gives ~2–3x inference speedup with small quality delta.
- Batching: keep interactive workloads at batch_size=1 for minimal queuing. For predictable throughput, run a small number of parallel workers per GPU (we recommend 4–6 workers depending on GPU).
- KV/prefix caching: enable automatic prefix caching for repeated system prompts — reduces per-request compute.
- Kernel profile: enable streaming-optimized kernels that prioritize first-token compute. This usually reduces p95 TTFT by ~20–30ms vs generic kernels.
- Networking: WebSocket or SSE both ok from a protocol perspective; WebSocket gives bi-directional control (useful for partial inputs/cancel), SSE is simpler for server->client streaming. Both supported by our runtime.

Sizing notes (initial PoC guidance):
- Target p95 TTFT <=70ms: provision pre-warmed pool of ~8 workers on A100-like nodes (example sizing, we’ll finalize after load testing).
- Concurrency: to cover 200 concurrent sessions with p95 TTFT headroom, plan for ~3–4 GPUs in dedicated cluster (depends on model choice).
- Chunk cadence: we optimize for first chunk within target TTFT; subsequent chunk cadence is a function of token-generation speed and network RTT. Our empirical guidance: with the above config you should see inter-chunk gaps of ~60–140ms for 8–16 token chunks on a low-latency path.

Logging/SLOs we’ll surface in the PoC dashboard: per-request TTFT (p50/p95/p99), inter-chunk delta distribution, concurrency, and queuing time.

Action: I’ll put together a short PoC runbook and a sizing worksheet (ETA EOD Tue). If you can share a small representative prompt set and expected average output lengths that’ll help dial the numbers.

—Dylan

Thanks Dylan — that’s useful. A couple quick infra notes from our side:

- We operate behind a WAF and terminate TLS at the edge (CloudFront/AKAMAI). We’ll need a short checklist for websocket sticky sessions and connection timeouts.
- Network RTT to Redwood region (us-west-2) from our primary users (us-east) is ~20–40ms; overall path should support the chunk cadence targets if TTFT is met.
- For the PoC we can provide a test harness (k6-based) and a small set of sample prompts. We’ll also want tracing headers propagated so we can map user sessions to Redwood request IDs for debugging.

Request: please include a short SLO matrix (p50/p95 p99 targets, measurement windows) and a minimal runbook for failover behavior. Also confirm if you support graceful fallback to a smaller quantized variant without changing API surface.

—Ryan
